A.explanation: 600 N ignores the 150 N share of the 300 N uniform plank acting at X, and 0 N wrongly assumes the plank weight has no effect when the child is at Y.

B.explanation: 600 N is only the child weight at X and misses the additional $150 \text{ N}$ from the plank weight supported at X.

C.explanation: 750 N is correct for the child at X, but 0 N is wrong because the uniform 300 N plank still needs $150 \text{ N}$ at X when the child is at Y.

D.explanation: Taking moments about Y gives $F = 750 \text{ N}$ with the 600 N child at X and $F = 150 \text{ N}$ with the child at Y.

hints: Notice the 4.0 m uniform plank weighs 300 N, so its weight acts at its centre 2.0 m from X and 2.0 m from Y.
Take moments about support Y so the force at Y has zero moment and $F$ at X can be found from the clockwise moments of the plank and child.
Compare the moment arm of the 600 N child: 4.0 m from Y when at X, but zero from Y when at Y, while the plank always contributes $300 \times 2.0$.
walkthrough: The plank is in equilibrium, so resultant force is zero and resultant moment about any point is zero. The uniform 300 N weight acts at the midpoint, $2.0 \text{ m}$ from X and $2.0 \text{ m}$ from Y.
Take moments about Y to eliminate the unknown force at Y. Anticlockwise moment is $F \times 4.0 \text{ m}$ and clockwise moments are from the plank and the child.
Child at X: child distance from Y is $4.0 \text{ m}$. So $F \times 4.0 = (600 \times 4.0) + (300 \times 2.0) = 2400 + 600 = 3000$. Hence $F = 3000/4.0 = 750 \text{ N}$.
Child at Y: child distance from Y is $0$, so it has no moment about Y. So $F \times 4.0 = (600 \times 0) + (300 \times 2.0) = 600$. Hence $F = 600/4.0 = 150 \text{ N}$.
750 N when the child is at X and 150 N when the child is at Y. This is option D.
